common_name: Veerle Mountain Hydrangea (Compact Violet-Blue Lacecap Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to partial sun; a Belgian-bred compact selection well suited to patio containers as well as borders.

directions: Veerle is a rounded, compact mountain hydrangea bred in Belgium that produces flat, airy lacecap heads of violet-blue fertile florets ringed by showy sterile rays from early summer well into fall, with flower tone shifting toward pink or purple as soil pH rises. Its unusually long bloom window and dense, well-branched form make it a reliable choice for smaller gardens, hedging, or large pots where a sprawling macrophylla would outgrow the space. Foliage turns bright red and orange in autumn, adding a second season of interest after bloom fades. Because it flowers mainly on old wood, limit pruning to shaping cuts right after flowering and keep soil evenly moist through summer heat.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Rosalba Mountain Hydrangea (Heirloom Crimson-Eyed Lacecap Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to partial shade; an old Japanese-origin cultivar long grown in European collections.

directions: Rosalba is a historic mountain hydrangea with slender, upright stems and narrow ovate leaves that carry flat lacecap heads whose sterile ray florets open white and age to rose or deep carmine, with inner fertile flowers staying rose to purple-blue rather than true blue even in acid soil. This fixed pigment pattern makes it a useful reference cultivar for breeders and a reliable color performer for gardeners who want consistent pink-and-white flowers regardless of soil pH. Narrower leaves than Hydrangea macrophylla give it a lighter, more refined texture in a shaded border, and foliage reddens attractively in fall. Prune only to remove spent wood just after flowering, since buds form the prior season.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade; valued as much for stem color as for bloom.

directions: Kurohime — whose name translates roughly to 'black princess' — is a mountain hydrangea grown chiefly for its glossy, deep purple-black stems, which stay showy through winter after the leaves drop. Flat lacecap flower heads emerge more intensely pigmented than most serrata cultivars, ranging from rose-pink to magenta or blue-purple depending on soil acidity, and the narrow foliage turns a vivid red in autumn. Its compact, well-branched habit suits a shaded border or woodland edge where the dark stems can be appreciated up close. Keep soil consistently moist and prune lightly right after bloom, since flowers set on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Okan Mountain Hydrangea (Golden-Leaf Mountain Hydrangea, PP14970)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade; strongest leaf-gold color develops out of harsh afternoon sun.

directions: Okan is a patented mountain hydrangea (U.S. Plant Patent PP14,970) selected by Hines Nurseries chiefly for its foliage: leaves emerge and hold a golden-yellow to chartreuse color through the growing season, making it a foliage accent as much as a flowering shrub. Its mounding, obliquely spreading habit stays compact, reaching roughly a meter in height and width at maturity over four to five years. Flat lacecap flower clusters appear against the bright foliage in early summer, with ray-floret color shifting from pink toward blue-violet on more acidic soil. Give it bright shade rather than full sun, since intense light can scorch the chartreuse leaves, and keep soil evenly moist through summer.

common_name: Intermedia Mountain Hydrangea (Dwarf Non-Blueing Lacecap Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to partial shade; stays noticeably smaller than most garden hydrangeas.

directions: Intermedia is a diminutive, slow-growing mountain hydrangea that rarely tops four feet, with thin, erect to gently spreading branches and lacecap heads whose ray florets stay in the pink-to-rose range rather than turning blue even in acidic soil, grouping it with 'Rosalba' among the species' fixed-color garden forms. Its small scale and early, dependable flowering make it a good fit for compact borders or container culture where larger macrophylla and serrata selections would crowd the space. Foliage is finer-textured than typical hydrangea leaves and colors modestly in fall. Water regularly during establishment and prune only to remove old flower heads, since next year's buds already form on the current season's wood by late summer.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
